Skywalker BY JOE FORDHAM W then Philippe Petit was 18 years old, an article in Paris Match magazine attracted his attention with an illustration of a pair of gigantic structures under construction on the shore of New York City's Hudson River. The World Trade Center towers haunted the young Frenchman who, at the time, was training to become a street entertainer and funambulist - from the Latin, 'rope walker.' When Petit visited America, the sight of the almostcompleted quarter-mile-high buildings became an obsession until, a week before his 25th birthday, he mounted his 'coup.' Surreptitiously stringing a 138-foot cable between the North and South Towers, Petit walked the wire eight times, without a safety harness. The image of Petit perched between the Twin Towers went on to become a poster image for the 2008 Academy Award-winning documentary, Man on Wire, directed by James March, which chronicled Petit's story. The documentary was one of several accounts of Petit's high-wire walk that, since the 2001 destruction of the World Trade Center buildings, came to represent an act of transcendent bravery that percolated pop culture. In 2002, Petit published his own vivid memoir, To Reach the Clouds, and in 2003, Mordicai 1 / 29 Gerstein published The Man Who Walked Between the Towers, a fairytale-like picture

THE WALK book that spawned an animated short film and a ballet. It was Gerstein's book that caught the eye of filmmaker Robert Zemeckis. "It was a children's book," said Zemeckis, "but I thought, 'Wow, that's interesting,' and when I researched the story, I discovered it was quite amazing. We bought Philippe's rights and, three years before Man on Wire appeared, we were well into designing our film, because we did it in a strange way. The most powerful part of Philippe's story was the walk, but I felt that would not translate effectively to the page as a screenplay. My decision was to create an animatic to present the story in the most powerful way possible. Zemeckis interviewed Petit and, using Petit's narration, fashioned an animatic with a pool of artists at his own studio, ImageMovers Digital, led by The Third Floor previsualization supervisor Eric Carney. "It was an hour-and-50-minute previs of the movie," recalled visual effects supervisor Kevin Baillie, who was part of the ImageMovers team. "It showed everything from Philippe's inspiration as a child all the way through his walk between the Twin Towers. It was such a powerful way of conveying Bob's vision for the film. It contained the DNA of the story and was a very clear communication of what he intended to show on screen." Walt Disney Pictures expressed interest in the project as an animated film, akin to Zemeckis' The Polar Express, Beowulf and A Christmas Carol. iWe briefly thought that we might do it as a performance capture movie," Robert Zemeckis explained. "That was because I always wanted to design this as a 3D movie and, back then, the most advanced 3D technology was in digital cinema. Prior to that, filmmakers had always created 3D by 2 / 29 bending light optically through two cameras, but I felt that optical 3D always had issues

with depth of field, whereas with digital 3D we could dial in depth of field wherever we wanted it to be. Luckily, it turned into a situation where technology caught up to the idea potential. TriStar was looking for risky stories with visionary filmmakers to be made on a responsible budget," recalled Kevin Baillie. "This movie fit into that mold. We were able to budget it so it could be done for a very reasonable price. We shot and did a lot of postproduction in Montreal, and tax credits there were very helpful. Beyond that, there was a lot of clever figuring out, on everybody's part, how to mold the scope of the movie to the budget." The film's screenplay, by Zemeckis and Christopher Browne, followed Petit (Joseph Gordon-Levitt) through his adolescence in France, his romantic partnership with Annie Allix (Charlotte Le Bon) and his mentorship with high-wire expert 'Papa' Rudy Omankowsky (Ben Kingsley). The story interspersed impressionistic flashbacks with a heist-like tale of Petit's struggles in Manhattan, 1974, to unite accomplices and hatch a plan to scale and traverse the Twin Towers, all the while dodging World Trade Center authorities. While Montreal offered facsimiles for areas of New York and Paris, the city had no equivalent for the World Trade Center towers, which loomed large almost as characters in their own right. "Philippe spoke to the towers as if they were living, breathing things," commented Robert Zemeckis.iHe had tremendous reverence toward them, and he perTHE WALK he project faltered when Disney parted ways with ImageMovers, but resurfaced as a live-action feature when Sony/TriStar chairman and chief executive officer Tom Rothman reviewed the animatic and recognized the material's dramatic 3 / 29

THE WALK sonalized them, like any artist does with their subject. It got to a point where Philippe called them 'his' towers, and he thought they were built for him. My criteria for the towers were they had to be absolutely real, and they had to look exactly the way they looked when Philippe did the walk. Then we could flex our creative muscles, deciding how we were going to paint the sky and how the light would change during the walk. Production designer Naomi Shohan collaborated with visual effects to discuss methods for building the towers. ¿The animatic played a strong role in helping determine how we were going to make this movie,i noted visual effects producer Camille Cellucci. "Bob was very clear about what he wanted, and Kevin had been on location scouts and taken copious notes and pictures. There was a tendency to say, 'I know, visual effects will do it!' But sometimes it was more economical to build practical set pieces, without relying on greenscreen. There was constant negotiation between departments, but what made it possible was that the departments supported each other. We all had to hit that same number." The filmmakers resolved to build partial sets at Mel's Cité du Cinéma, and then combine them with digital extensions representing 110 floors of aluminum, glass and steel, an expansive stone plaza and a soaring lobby of cathedral-like windows.iNaomi had some great researchers in her art department," said Kevin Baillie. "We had plans for every floor of both World Trade Center towers, and then we went to town looking for every image of the area that we could find. As we progressed, Bob modified a few details of the building layout to help the story. For example, our World Trade Center lobby was accurate, 4 / 29 but we took a few liberties with where characters entered. To anyone familiar with the

towers, it felt authentic, but it also worked for our story." Atomic Fiction, which Baillie co-founded with Ryan Tudhope in Oakland, led creation of the towers, working in collaboration with its newly established studio in Montreal and two other vendors. For ground-based scenes, Rodeo FX extended a set of one-eighth of the South Tower façade and a portion of the lobby surrounded by greenscreen, and also provided extensions for other scenes set around New York City. Universal Production Partners, in Prague, contributed to extensions within the towers' upper levels, and scenes set in France. extended digitally by Atomic Fiction. For scenes in the incomplete office space below the rooftop - temporary refuge for Petit and his collaborators on their covert missions infiltrating the building - the production implemented a space-saving measure by constructing a 60x40-foot section of the 110th floor directly beneath the rooftop set. UPP then created digital extensions to expand the area into a 200x200-foot space. To lay groundwork for re-creating 1974 New York City, the production conducted aerial surveys above the present day site of Petit's walk. "We did two days of aerial shooting above Manhattan in a helicopter," said Baillie. "We had clearance to overfly the Freedom Tower and the site where the World Trade Center towers once stood, and we hovered in the exact place where Philippe did his walk. The thought that Philippe really walked there, on a wire, without any safety equipment, made my adrenaline spike and, at the same time, made me sick to my stomach. It was an incredible experience. Baillie captured high-resolution digital still images using a handheld Canon 5D Mark III and a RED Epic camera, with a 6K Dragon sensor, attached to a gyro-stabilized mount on the nose of the aircraft. The imagery served as reference for a fully 3D digital re-creation of a square mile of the city, with 21⁄2D matte paintings beyond that, accurate to the time period. Atomic Fiction began CG city construction using a commercially available model of Manhattan, together with satellite surveys and an online gallery - Urban Layers - that displayed historical comparisons of New York City structures. The website had a slider that allowed us to scroll back and forth revealing what buildings were built at what dates, related Baillie. When we referenced that to our footage and maps of Manhattan, we determined what we could use from our reference photos. A lot of modern buildings have obscured older buildings that were in plain sight in 1974. In some cases, we had to build CG versions of period buildings, particularly where those buildings were iconic to the 1974 skyline. The need for three-dimensional architecture compelled Atomic artists to create New York City extensions that were far more render-intensive than they initially anticipated.iWe realized we needed a 3D-asset-based approach to lower Manhattan rather than a mattepainted approach," commented associate visual effects supervisor Jim Gibbs. "A large part of my role involved wrangling city asset development, consolidating our visual research and pulling in as many artists as we could to start building historically accurate 6 / 29 buildings. The city ended up pretty much all 3D by the time we were done with it. We

used a lot of Kevin's aerial plates to texture roofs and some streets, and then for areas further off we used reference images and procedural texturing to give the matte painters a base to start from. We covered 12 city blocks that radiated from the World Trade Center towers. Closer sections had four buildings per block; more distant sections each had 10 to 15 buildings. Beyond that, we used texture projections as '21⁄2D Manhattan,' and in the distance we used procedural and matte-painted textures." environment supervisor Brian Flora. For example, as Philippe set up his wire, the sun was just below the horizon, which was a 'hopeful' color palette." The paintings served as color bibles for each sequence.iWe took a hero render from key moments in the walk, aligned those with soundstage plates and made Photoshop paintings to represent the mood, adding subtle washes of light, atmosphere and color. Once Robert Zemeckis gave his blessing, we implemented those effects, and our compositors matched those subtle looks and added atmosphere. To help that process, one of our lead compositors, Jed Smith, came up with a way to make 21⁄2D gradient maps based on z-depth, which allowed him to mesh all the colors in the atmosphere and match them to our concept paintings. That gave compositors a starting point to quickly get each shot in the ballpark. "We didn't want to create a heavy local rendering infrastructure. If you have downtime between projects, you have to pay for that equipment, so you end up loading the next show with that cost. "If we had simply replicated the towers, section by identical section," observed Jim Gibbs, "they would have looked fake. Instead, we split the towers into levels. Often, we only needed the top corner of a tower in shot, so we detailed those areas, going back and forth with our modelers THE WALK o manage the enormous scale of digital set extension work, lead developer Greg Denton used Atomic Fiction's cloud-rendering tool - ConductorlO - with Google's Compute Engine. THE WALK and texture artists, and made sure there were imperfections in the surfaces. We wanted the metal to feel real, while retaining the feeling that the towers were brand new, because they were in the final stages of construction when Philippe did his walk. Once we achieved that level of refinement - with slightly beveled edges, little bits of chaos in the paneling, and 3D 'warbles' of irregular reflections - we rolled those textures down the tower and staggered them in what we called a 'Tetris' pattern. Whenever the camera was peering up the tower it saw slight imperfections in paneling, creating the impression of how the tower was put together in pieces." Atomic Fiction constructed the Twin Towers in Autodesk Maya, The Foundry's Mari, Modo, Katana and Chaos Group V-Ray, referencing archival images of the towers' material properties. "The towers were chameleon-like," noted Kevin Baillie. "They were clad in anodized aluminum, so when it was sunny they looked one way, and when it was cloudy they looked completely different." A new development in V-Ray's GGX shading model allowed Atomic to use environmental effects to illuminate reflective surfaces.iOnce we textured the towers, we used V-Ray's tools to bake in global illumination. GGX simulated all the little micro bumps in the aluminum surfaces, and all of a sudden it looked right. To show off the majesty of the towers in vertiginous perspectives, the production plotted stereoscopic conversions with Legend3D, working first with on-set stereoscopic supervisor Matt DeJohn, who spent two weeks gathering reference material that would later assist stereoscopic conversions from single-camera photography. Zemeckis committed to going 'all in' with the 3D - both on the towers, and in more 10 / 29 intimate character scenes - and developed a cinematic language with Legend3D in real-

THE WALK time interactive viewing sessions via T-VIPS, a video image sharing system owned by Nevion. "It was a massive amount of 3D," said Legend3D stereoscopic supervisor Jared Sandrew. Bob's goal was to use stereo composition to direct the viewer's eye based on the sensibility of each scene. We gave the film a lot of volume and pushed the overall depth budget using our projection technology to make it as immersive as possible. We wanted to make sure that when Philippe was standing on top of the World Trade Center, the building looked massive and everything beyond felt small in comparison, so we animated the interaxial - expanding the distance between the right- and left-eye cameras - so volumes appeared to expand. Bob's filmmaking style played into that. There were only 840 shots in the movie, so they were lengthy, and many were composed with wideangle lenses. That meant there was a lot of detail in frame, and the viewer's eye had a chance to really investigate the scenes." Legend3D created stereo effects by analyzing two-dimensional image sequences, and then assigning volume budgets for scenes over several months. First, we isolated what shapes we needed for characters and objects in each shot," said Sandrew. "Then we did our region design process, creating 2D representations of our 3D models. We made a mesh for each object, and imagined how much volume we'd need, which determined the resolution of the mesh. Bob viewed scenes in continuity, with audio, so he could tell us if a character's volume felt natural to him, or if the towers needed more stature, and we manipulated depth values in real time. A lot of psychology went into that design, so it was helpful to have interactive sessions with the filmmaker. I1 / 29 Pixelgun Studio conducted on-site scans, surrounding performers with an array of

80 digital cameras to capture photogrammetry data of facial geometry and skin textures. Pixelgun material added to the fidelity of Legend3D's facial depth simulations, and allowed Atomic Fiction to assist wire-walk scenes, blending Joseph Gordon-Levitt's face to his stunt double. "Wire-walking is not a skill you can learn overnight," noted Kevin Baillie. "But Joe was an amazingly fit and talented guy, and Bob got him to train for ten days with Philippe. Joe was able to do an impressive number of his own scenes on the wire in our rooftop set, wearing a safety harness; and then a Cirque Du Soleil performer, Jade Kindar-Martin, did more complicated moves. We then did 37 digital face replacements, putting Joe's face on Jade. and gave us a lot more control, so we reworked our pipeline for that, and when we implemented the Pixelgun textures of Joe's face in closeup turntable images, the results were incredible. Atomic tested the face model with a shot of Kindar-Martin enacting one of Petit's street performances, balancing on one foot on a line strung between two light poles, while juggling. 'That was a stunt that Joe couldn't do, and I'm sure even most street performers couldn't accomplish. The camera began up high over Jade, who was looking up, and then it descended. We replaced Jade's face with Joe's, and it was a pretty hero shot." V-Ray's skin shader had a fast subsurface scattering system that we hadn't tried before," recalled Jim Gibbs. "That was effective 12 / 29

'The great thing about that was it also gave us perfectly aligned color texture data of Joe's skin. When Joe winced, we could have the blood leave his forehead and create a pale forehead while his cheeks became rosy. It was not just about the form of the face - it contained subtleties of color, which created very realistic feelings of emotion." Wherever possible, Gordon-Levitt performed on the wire, wearing moccasin slippers with padded-leather soles, while he carried a 26-foot balancing pole. A safety cable extended from a harness around his waist. Untethered wire-walking remained the heart of the performance. He started two feet up, and then we increased the height as he gained more confidence. He ended up being able to walk the wire 100 feet in a straight line, 20 feet up. When he was filming, he wore his safety line, but we did not pull on it too much, so he was free-walking until we saw he was in trouble. That happened only one time during a take - Joe was about to fall so he laid into 13 / 29 his harness and we picked him up. Otherwise, Joe was walking by himself.

We spent three days with still cameras and a movie camera, and shot many streets in different districts that we used as elements." Paris extensions included augmentations of building façades and distant views of the Eiffel Tower, which UPP created by removing modern lighting fixtures from photographic textures of the landmark, which they projected onto a 3D model. For scenes of Petit's street performances, juggling on a unicycle, Joseph GordonLevitt rode a rickshaw-like contraption that stunt technicians pushed. 'The unicycle was bolted onto a 12-foot pole," said Marc Désourdy. "Two stunt guys held on to that and ran alongside, balancing it for Joe. The special effects team also connected the unicycle to a golf cart, and they gave that a small suspension system to create a smoother bounce. UPP added background extensions and face replacements where Jade Kindar-Martin doubled for Petit. Joseph Gordon-Levitt performed juggling with balls and fire-sticks; UPP added to the airborne objects, multiplying balls and one additional fire-stick. In flashback, Petit recalls his experience as a boy (Soleyman Pierini) becoming enamored with a circus high-wire performer (Jade Kindar-Martin), and his subsequent attempts to walk an improvised line at his country home. "Philippe strung a rope between two trees in his backyard," related Kevin Baillie. "Getting that to work was a big challenge for the special effects and props teams. It involved three people standing behind camera, handing young Philippe different ropes at different times in order to create a time-lapse 15 / 29 view of the boy setting up his walk. We shot that against greenscreen, and then Rodeo FX

built an idyllic French backyard digital environment around it. greenscreen, and a stunt double falling into a pond in the parking lot at Mel's. UPP shot backgrounds in a small village outside Paris and stylized the sequence like a dream.iIt wasn't supposed to be super realistic," said Viktor Muller, "but we tried to use real elements, such as trees with moving leaves, to make it look natural. Originally, Bob thought it could be told with still frames, but after he cut the scene together he changed it to full motion. It was a challenge to make the stunt of Philippe falling work with our moving plates, because the stunt was shot from a different perspective, with different water levels and reflections. To align Philippe's splash, UPP excavated a trench, filled it with water, and then used it to stage elements of water splashes against bluescreen. We didn't want the water to look 'fake' in any way that a viewer might mistake for bad CG. So as Philippe hit the water, we rotoscoped the figure from the plate and replaced the water with our new element and just a few CG elements in the composite.i Petit's memories of France culminate in his recollection of his first major wire-walking stunt in 1971, traversing a wire between the towers of Notre Dame cathedral. The production built a minimal greenscreen set to represent the Paris walk. iIt was the tiniest set you've ever seen," noted Kevin Baillie. "We had ten feet of railing, four or five feet high. Everything else was built at UPP." THE WALK or Philippe Petit's first public wire-walk, traversing an inclined line strung across a small pond, the production staged the scene in Montreal using combinations of Gordon-Levitt's performance, walking the Canadian beam on a slope against 16 / 29

THE WALK UPP spent a day and night photographing the Gothic architecture masterpiece.iNotre Dame has two towers," Viktor Muller explained. "The south side is the Tourist Tower, and the north side is the Bishop's Tower. We were very lucky because we had access to the Bishop's Tower, which is normally private. We were able to climb out onto the roof and shoot all the elements we needed. We then re-created that environment for a very tricky shot. Wrinkles in Time BY JODY DUNCAN n one of the most iconic scenes in the history of motion pictures, Arnold Schwarzenegger, in his buffed-up prime, stands at the window of a police precinct office, and solemnly intones, "I'll be back." Indeed, he was. After the spectacular success of 1984's low-budget The Terminator, written and directed by a then unknown James Cameron, Schwarzenegger returned as the Terminator seven years later in Terminator 2: Judgment Day, also co-written and directed by Cameron, and then again in the 2003 Terminator: Rise of the Machines, directed by Jonathan Mostow. Only in McG's 2009 film, Terminator Salvation, starring Christian Bale, was Schwarzenegger absent. Having dispatched his duties as governor of California, Schwarzenegger returns in Terminator Genisys, the fifth entry in the Terminator saga. Neither a sequel to the previous movies nor a remake, Terminator Genisys is the product of producer David Ellison's and director Alan Taylor's efforts to re-launch the franchise by returning to its roots, to characters and ideas introduced in the first two films, through the conceit of an alter1 / 28 nate timeline that hops from the years 2029 to 1984 to 2017.

TERMINATOR 5 Ellison, Taylor and their production crews shot the film in New Orleans, followed by a few days in San Francisco at the end of the principal photography schedule. Visual effects crews, under the guidance of visual effects supervisor Janek Sirrs, remained in San Francisco for a month after the shoot had wrapped, photographing stills and plates that would provide the foundation of an all-CG city for purposes of digital extensions and destruction featured in the film's third act. Terminator Genisys opens with a brief titles sequence recounting 'Judgment Day,' the day that the computer system, Skynet, becomes self-aware and launches a global nuclear attack against mankind. The montage of images, realized by Industrial Light & Magic, starts with a wide view of launching missiles, then follows with closer shots of the destruction of San Francisco. ILM visual effects supervisor Grady Cofer and his team found inspiration in the Judgment Day sequence from Terminator 2.iNot only is that one of the great iconic scenes in visual effects history," remarked Cofer, "but, in this case, we were going to be destroying San francisco, our hometown. We attacked the sequence with a fair amount of enthusiasm.i Using location plates shot by Janek Sirrs, ILM animation supervisor Scott Benza first blocked out the sequence in post-vis, adding multiple layers of animated destruction as suggested by the 'Nukemap' website. "Nukemap allows you to enter a map location and a kiloton yield," explained Cofer. "Then, based on that information, it shows you how much of the city would be enveloped in the fireball, as well as the location of the thermal and outer pressure radii. Janek wanted the nuclear blast to be based on science, and so 2 / 28 we carefully distinguished between the thermal blast, which is practically instantaneous,

and the pressure wave, which follows later." Using flight animation tools first developed at ILM in 2000 for Pearl Harbor, Scott Benza choreographed the arrival of the nuclear warheads based on intercontinental ballistic missile trajectories, and then blocked in the nuclear destruction of San Francisco using simplified geometry and rigid body simulations. "The animation was just a template that would be used to drive the effects and rigid body sims, anyway," said Benza, "so we wanted the post-vis animation to be based on real physics. That way, when the rigid body simulation team came in, it wouldn't be trying to match something that was not possible from a physics standpointi there in it, with buildings collapsing around us and firewalls washing over usiiTo create the digital San Francisco, the visual effects team lidar-scanned large swaths of the city's Columbus and California Streets, and also captured high dynamic range panoramas at every scanning location. ILM then sent that massive data set to its partner, Virtuos, in Shanghai, where city blocks were modeled and textured. Virtuos also modeled the Trans America Building, targeted for destruction in the sequence, while modelers from both Virtuos and ILM tackled the Golden Gate Bridge. All of the city structures were then prepped for destruction, with teams adding interior architectural features such as cables and pieces of metal framework that would be TERMINATOR 5 he destruction of San Francisco, seen at street level, required authentic CO versions of its structures and landmarks. "This was a new take on Judgment Day," said Grady Cofer, iin that, rather than see it all from a distance, we are right 3 / 28

revealed in the blast. "Once the buildings were prepped," said Cofer, "we took them into TERMINATOR 5I our proprietary Zeno tool for fracturing and demolition sims. These were combined with flipping car sims, asphalt fractures - everything we could think of - and then all of those simulations were cached out and brought into Autodesk's 3ds Max for look development. Rendering was done in Chaos' V-Ray. "V-Ray does an amazing job at rendering complex scenes, and the complexity of this destruction scene was astounding. One shot alone, looking up California Street, had about 780 million polygons being rendered together. ILM used Side Effects Houdini and its proprietary Plume software to create attendant smoke, fire and shattered glass effects. Plume was instrumental in creating a particular feature of the blast, nicknamed 'Benza's fingers,' which has roiling smoke and fire reaching between buildings - inspired by similar shots in Jim Cameron's original Judgment Day sequence in Terminator 2. "The idea," said Cofer, "was that the surface explosion would create this expanding platter of fire, but as the platter squeezed between the buildings, it would become fingers slicing down the streets. By separating those fingers, Scott Benza was able to carefully choreograph the fire's speed and timing. The result was that each shot had its own dramatic build up." A final blast near the Golden Gate Bridge sends a tidal wave of San Francisco Bay water outward in concentric circles. "We simulated a cubic kilometer of water," said Cofer. "It upends a cargo ship and launches hundreds of shipping containers into the air, and then that pressure wave blasts through the bridge, crumbling the tarmac and 4 / 28 causing cables to snap. The water was done separately in Houdini, but we were able to

combine all of the other rigid and cable sims in Zeno, in a multi-physics scenario. Once we had simulated a complex swinging motion and the breaking of the bridge, that was handed off to our water sim artist, Roman Schmidt, who then used it for collisions with his tidal waves. Water rushes over the lens, and the camera is enveloped in a volume of super-heated steam. 'That's when the main title comes up. Out of that main title, we do a nice time-dissolve to the next scene, which is the aftermath M against Skynet's machines. #The work camp is our version of the battle scene that James Cameron never got to film," commented Janek Sirrs. So, it's basically a war sequence, which we shot on a big empty lot in New Orleans." Special effects supervisor Mark Hawker and his crew were on set to generate battle pyrotechnics. The puppets and stop-motion work in Terminator resulted in endoskeleton movement that was a little stiff and clunkyi com6 / 28 mented Janek Sirrs. iWe wanted to update that look and make it more sophisticated;

but, we knew that if we strayed too far from its behavior in the first movie, it wouldn't feel like the same character. We had to find the balance between nostalgia for the original and the sophisticated animation that is possible now - and that took some time. M some shots, they had to move very fast; in others, they were more static. In every shot, regardless of what the endoskeleton was doing, MPC had to take into consideration the fact that an endoskeleton is, at its core, a robot trying to mimic human motion. We had to find the line where robotic, mechanical movement met more organic movement. So we explored both extremes, and then found a middle ground that made the endoskeleton machine-like, and yet believable as something trying to look human. MPC generated other effects for the work camp sequence, as well, including augmenting the live pyrotechnics and expanding the camp set. As it was designed, the work camp was supposed to be located in Los Angeles, at LAX airport. So the requirement was to sell that location in wide aerial shots, and to make it clearly recognizable as LAX." We went through a process of designing what all of these cells and structures would look like, and then TERMINATOR 5 PC explored endoskeleton behaviors in a series of animation studies. The idea was to make the new design aspects cool, but also functional. ¿Still, we always cross-referenced the original movies and tried to capture the unique characteristics of these pieces of hardware. Keeping It Real Mission: Impossible - Rogue Nation We at Cinefex have always prided ourselves on presenting our readers with the very best in visual effects journalism, illustrated with the very best imagery, often exclusive. In recent years, procuring that imagery has become increasingly problematic, due in large part to a proliferation of approval authorities at the studio, production and talent levels, all empowered to kill an image for whatever reason. Or no reason. In accordance with studio protocol, all of the visual effects companies involved in Mission: Impossible - Rogue Nation submitted images representing their best work, earmarked for us, to Paramount Pictures. Virtually none of it was approved — only a few incidental shots non-representative of the work and having little or nothing to do with our article. What we were provided, instead, were stock presskit images, including non-effects movie-star shots, artfully faked still composites, and a few digitally falsified behindthe-scenes' photos. After countless requests for reconsideration, by us and by others on our behalf, all to no avail, we were forced at last to admit defeat - for the first time in our 35-year history. We could have saved face by pulling the article entirely. But it's a terrific piece, on a fine film with great effects, and so we are going ahead with it. Rather than insult our readers by illustrating the article with patently dishonest photography, however, we have opted to present it without imagery. Another first. Hopefully the last.

Double Negative also contributed to a sequence set at an opera house in Vienna, where Ethan Hunt attempts to stop Syndicate henchmen from assassinating the Austrian chancellor. "Main unit went to Vienna, and shot at the Vienna Opera House," explained Vickery. Constraints were such that we couldn't actually shoot on their stage - so we couldn't shoot the opera that is going on in the film, which was Puccini's Turandot, or the fight that takes place backstage and above the stage - but we were able to shoot the front of the house and the auditorium. We shot a crowd of about 50 people sitting in multiple positions in the auditorium, the idea being that we would then replicate the crowd to fill all 2,500 seats. Then we built the entire Opera House stage and backstage areas on a stage in West London, so we could shoot the opera itself, and the fight scene with Tom hanging on a trestle 40 feet up in the air, with the opera going on beneath him. Every shot of that fight looking out into the auditorium area was just greenscreen, so we had to 18 / 27 build a digital environment to piece the London stage together with the Viennese auditor-

ium. It was a bit of a jigsaw, with crowd replication and digital environment extensions. The digital environment extensions were built from photographs and surveys of the Vienna Opera House captured by CG supervisor Dan Neal. iDan went out to Vienna and made sure we got that as a full asset that we could reconstruct back here at Double Negative," said Ken Hahn, "not only the building, but the entire opera house auditorium, with all of the necessary crowd replications. On the day, Dan had photographed all the extras from many different angles on a digital video camera, and then we rotoscoped off them and plopped them into seats as needed. There were also some locked-off tiles they shot of people in the seats, which worked for some of the angles, but not for othersi wanted to get the full audience appreciation and enthusiastic applause for the opera that they just saw, and so we shot a set of crowd plates at Leavesden, against greenscreen, with 90 extras. We'd shoot the first set of 90 people in a very specific order, get them changed out of the costumes and then reposition our cameras to get them all in the appropriate spaces for that particular shot. And then we shot four pick-ups as singles, doubles and triples to put in some of the balconies, as well as some of the other shots that we needed." In addition to augmenting the crowd and piecing together shots filmed at two different locations, Double Negative extended the trestle area above the stage where Ethan M:| 5 rews shot additional crowd pickups later on a greenscreen stage at Leavesden. "That's where we shot a lot of shot-specific stuff," explained Hahn, "such as a master shot at the end, when the opera hits the high note. Chris McQuarrie 19 / 27

"The stage set went up to the rafters, but there wasn't enough celling height above that to get the look of this fight going on very high above the stage where the opera is being performed. So we had to go in and replace the stage ceiling with an extension to create a much taller space. Throughout the film, the IMF agents use state-of-the-art tools to execute their mission, including masks that enable them to impersonate characters. Double Negative delivered a number of mask reveals for the film, again employing effects that were as invisible and subtle as possible.The mask reveals are one of the signature effects of the Mission: Impossible franchise," remarked David Vickery, "and they were a really fun part of the film for us." One of Chris McQuarrie's directives was that the CG component of any mask reveal not be apparent in the final shots.iNone of us wanted to do mask reveals where a CG head would suddenly take you out of the film," said Vickery. "Chris also didn't want there to be apparent cheats. He'd seen mask shots in previous films where there was a trick of some kind - wiping behind somebody's back in order to hide the key moment when the mask was being removed, for example, or locking the camera off in order to make the effects work simpler. Chris's feeling was that the audience is sophisticated enough in this day and age to understand that when you see a lock off, someone is cheating something, somewhere. The audience begins to get suspicious before the gag is given up. So Chris wanted us to come up with ideas and designs for these mask reveal shots that 20 / 27 would be new and exciting, and that weren't repetitive in any way. If we came up with an

idea for one mask reveal, we couldn't use the same technique for another. In one scene - ultimately deleted from the film - Benji removes a mask he has donned to impersonate CIA Director Hunley, played by Alec Baldwin. "On the day," recalled Vickery, "we had Simon Pegg in a body suit to make him bulkier, so he would match the frame and size and shape of Alec Baldwin. We shot one pass of Simon taking off an Alec Baldwin mask, which had been built to fit snugly over his face. That was our hero passi The practical mask was not usable for closer shots of Benji in disguise. ¿'The prosthetics artists make wonderfully detailed masks, but they don't look 100 percent real when you get close up. If you're full frame on a head, there's no way in the world you could make a mask that looks like a real human. They don't fool anyone unless you're ten feet away. So we couldn't use the practical mask up close, but it was fantastic reference for how the mask would deform as it came off, and how the silicone would movei sions, his movement and his body posture, without the rubber mask getting in the way. In a third pass, cameras recorded Alec Baldwin as he re-created Simon Pegg's body positions and head movements in the clean pass. A final pass captured Baldwin remaining still, without the head and body movements. "On the A side," said Vickery, "we had Alec Baldwin moving as if removing the mask, then we transitioned to Simon Pegg going through the same motions. We then projected the stationary element of Alec Baldwin onto M:I 5| rews then shot a second 'clean' pass, in which Simon Pegg pretended to take the mask off, but was not actually wearing it. 'That gave us is a completely clean, unoccluded view of Simon's head," said Vickery. "It gave us his facial expres21 / 27

M:I 5| the mask that Simon was wearing in the first pass, deforming it to the rubber mask as it was torn off. We built a 3D model of Alec's head, and a 3D model of Simon's head, and then we could project Alec's real face onto the mask and deform it as it was removed. And because the real rubber mask was there in that one pass, we got all the fantastic detail of rubber deformations and tears in the material as the mask was ripped offi For another shot in which Benji dons a mask to impersonate a businessman, Christopher McQuarrie tasked Vickery with achieving the transformation without any use of visual effects. "Chris said: 'I want to do one shot in camera,'" said Vickery. "I don't want to cheat in any way. No visual effects.'" In the shot, Benji is sitting in a chair in front of a full-frame mirror as Ethan Hunt puts the mask on him. You can see Ethan and Benji in the foreground, with Ilsa - Rebecca Ferguson - standing next to them, and they are all reflected in the mirror." To achieve the shot, McQuarrie suggested they build two sets - one a mirror image of the other. 'Between them was a wall with an empty frame where the mirror should be," said Vickery. "The detail in the reverse set was incredible. Actors' costumes had to be backward - even the books and CDs on the shelf in the background had to be backward. Every department did an incredible job. As cameras rolled, Simon Pegg sat on one side of the mirrored sets, and the actor he was impersonating sat on the other. Also in frame were body doubles for Cruise and Ferguson.iIt then became a simple matter of where to place everyone and, of course, the camera," said Vickery. "It took 20 takes to make sure Tom, Simon, Rebecca and their 22 / 27 doubles were doing the same actions at the same time. The finished shot was really ele-

M:| 5 gant, and it was all done in camera. It is still a visual effect, but it is old-school smoke and mirrors, without the smoke and, actually, without the mirror!i n another scene, the camera comes in close as Ethan Hunt removes a mask that has enabled him to impersonate a member of the Syndicate named Attlee. Chris wanted this shot to be a gentle, push-in reveal," said Graham Page, "even though it had originally been planned as a wipe. They were going to have an actor in the foreground, the camera was going to dolly around behind him, and that was going to give us a wipe to transition from Attlee to Ethan. But on the day, it was such a confined space that the camera move just wasn't going to fit in the scene, and so they switched it to a push-in. We shot a hero pass of Tom Cruise with the mask on, and then pulling it off. Then, in that same environment, we shot a pass of Attlee mimicking what Tom had done in his hero pass. Then we painted out Tom's head for the first part of the shot, and replaced that with a tracked-in version of Attlee's performance. The element of the Attlee performer was deemed too static, so Double Negative artists added some life to it by culling bits of movement from alternate takes. "We added a bit of a lip purse from one take," Page explained, "and blinks from another take, just to make it feel less rigid. It was quite a lot of work making sure the glasses moved as they should, and that the light moved through them appropriately. They were quite intricate pieces of compositing to make sure that they warped cor23 / 27 rectly and that there weren't any pops or roto problems. I remember that when we

M:I 5| presented those shots to Chris, he stepped through them very carefully to make sure that there was no cheating going on." It was then a case of tracking in the technician's face on top of the mask, with all of the usual warping to make it work. That was blended in with the mask through a sort of arm wipe - the arm comes across and reveals the original mask." One of Us, in London, created the graphics for the gait analysis device that blows Benji's cover. "With these kinds of graphics," stated One of Us visual effects supervisor Dominic Parker, iwe always want to illustrate the technical process they are depicting, but we also have to fulfill the storytelling required in the shot - and that means getting inside the director's head, and determining what he wants. We pan from one screen, which has the security camera that is analyzing Benji, to a screen that shows a point-cloud version of him as his gait, 24 / 27 the length of his stride, the length of his limbs, et cetera, are all being analyzed. To de-

velop the graphics, Parker and his team first researched real-world gait analysis technology. ¿Gait analysis is a real thing, much like facial recognition cameras, or even the smile recognition on your phone camera. One of Us also created graphics for the mask-making machine Benji employs to create his disguise. "Benji is thinking about how he might break into this building," said Parker, and we freeze-frame on him as he says, 'I could wear a mask,' and then dissolve into the process of building a mask from a set of photographs. M:I 5| concepts across in graphics. We only had 30 or 40 frames to tell the story of, 'Okay, this is a device that can pick a lock, and now it's inside the lock, and this is what is happening.' The details required to make that work were different than the usual visual effects challenges, because it was more about the storytelling than it was about the reality of it. The majority of the film's screen graphics were created by SPOV, a design and animation company in London, which had previously worked primarily within the videogame industry. Mission: Impossible - Rogue Nation was the firm's first big break into feature films. Like those at Double Negative and One of Us, the artists at SPOV strove to create graphics that were convincing and visually interesting, but also told a story. "Every frame existed to serve the narrative," said SPOV supervisor Allen Leitch. "They didn't want a lot of bells and whistles, or pretty for pretty's sake. Our contribution was all about moving the narrative forward." On-set screen graphics were provided by Compulire, but most were replaced by SPOV in post. "The on-set graphics team did a fantastic job," said Leitch, "but, often, they didn't have the time on set to make sure that what they were doing was precise, according to the story. Also, the story and the edit evolved; and so, what was right at the time of shooting was not necessarily right by the time we got to postproduction. SPOV also provided graphics for screens that had remained black or greenscreened on set. For all of its graphics, the company used a standard motion graphics pipeline.iOur pipeline is predominantly the Adobe suite, but we also use a product called Cinema4D a lot, as well as a few essential plug-ins. Our design pipeline is good old pen and paper! 26 / 27 Whatever we're using for the work, it is very much a team effort here, all orchestrated by

M:| 5 our amazing producer, Emma Middlemiss." One key sequence for SPOV was set in a record store, where Ethan Hunt is first briefed on the IMF's mission. "It is delivered in a new and interesting way," said Leitch. "It isn't your run-of-the-mill flat screen graphic, but rather a plausible holographic image. It still had to look achievable with current technology - or with technology that might be available in a few years' time. That is always the benchmark with a Mission: Impossible film: You take what's leading edge today, and push it a year or two beyond thati The reality-based graphics reflected Christopher McQuarrie's approach to every action sequence, mask reveal and visual effects shot in Mission: Impossible - Rogue Nation, which was to honor the franchise's tradition of films that are grounded in reality, with a minimum of digital chicanery. "Like a lot of directors," David Vickery noted, "Chris has a healthy skepticism about CG. Every one of us has seen too many films where the CG didn't look completely convincing - and that is especially problematic in a Mission: Impossible film, where the effects are supposed to be invisible. The rules, always, were: 'No cheating. No CG for CG's sake. Do it in camera. Keep it real."
